title: Reading Comprehension
summary: One 250–350-word passage with 5 questions in Tier 1; 3 passages (12–15 questions) in Tier 2. Passages come from editorials, science reporting and social issues, and every answer is traceable to a line. RC is the highest-value block in the English section — five marks for one fixed routine.

subtopics.title: How to attempt an RC passage in SSC exams
subtopics.concept:
An SSC reading-comprehension passage runs 250–350 words with 5 questions, and you get barely 6–8 minutes for the whole set. Speed comes from a fixed routine, not from reading faster in general.

**The SSC-tested routine (passage first, questions second):**
1. Read the passage once at full attention — about 2 minutes. You are reading for *structure*: what each paragraph does.
2. Read the questions (do not study all four options yet) — 30 seconds.
3. Return to the exact lines each question points to, and answer from those lines only.

Reading the passage first works better in SSC papers because questions constantly refer to "the author" and "the passage", and most details are asked in order of appearance, so one clean read lets you locate them from memory.

**Paragraph mapping.** As you finish each paragraph, tag it in three words: e.g. "para 1: cause of heat islands; para 2: who suffers; para 3: solutions". Detail answers then take seconds to find.

| Wrong habit | Why it fails | Do instead |
|---|---|---|
| Reading options before the passage | options plant false memories of "facts" | read passage first |
| Re-reading difficult sentences repeatedly | eats the clock, adds confusion | note the line number, move on, return only if a question asks |
| Answering from outside knowledge | the paper marks what is *written*, not what is true | every answer must be traceable to a line |
| Skipping the passage and matching keywords only | options paraphrase, so keywords mislead | use keywords to *reach* the line, then read the line |

**Time budget for a 5-question set:** first read ~2 min, questions ~20–30 s each, one final verification pass ~30 s. If a vocabulary-in-context question appears, do it first — it needs only its own sentence.

tricks.title: Two-minute structure read
tricks.body: On the first read, do not hunt for facts. After each paragraph say its job in three words. Facts are cheap to re-find; structure is what saves you.

tricks.title: Vocab questions first, main idea last
tricks.body: Answer the replace-the-word question and line-specific details before the main-idea question — by then you will have re-touched half the passage and the theme is clear.

example.q: A set has Q1 main idea, Q2 a detail from para 2, Q3 replace-the-word, Q4 inference, Q5 title.
example.solution: Attempt order: Q3 → Q2 → Q4 → Q1 → Q5. The two theme questions answered last use the understanding built by the others.

tricks.title: Line anchoring
tricks.body: Every detail question has a home line. Match a distinctive word in the question (a name, a number, an odd noun) to the passage, read two lines around it, and choose the option that paraphrases them.

mistakes: Answering from general knowledge because the option sounds true in real life.
Spending four minutes on the first read to 'understand everything' — the first read only maps the passage.
Leaving RC for the last two minutes; the 5-question set is the highest-value block in the section.
Choosing an option because it copies words from the passage even though its meaning differs.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a reading comprehension (RC)?
"Comprehension" means *understanding*. In an RC question you get a short passage (usually 200–350 words) and 4–6 questions on it. The exam is not testing your general knowledge. It is testing one skill: **can you find and understand what is written?** Every correct answer can be pointed to in the passage.

Think of RC like a train timetable. You do not memorise the whole timetable. You know where things are, and you go back to the right line when someone asks you a question.

### The 3-step routine
1. **Read the passage once, calmly (about 2 minutes).** Do not try to remember every fact. Just notice what each paragraph is doing.
2. **Read the questions.** Only the question line — not all the options yet.
3. **Go back to the exact lines** the question points to, answer from those lines, then look at the options.

### Paragraph mapping (the biggest time-saver)
After each paragraph, tell yourself its job in 3–5 words:
- Para 1: *problem — millets disappeared*
- Para 2: *why millets are useful now*
- Para 3: *what stops the revival*

Now a question like "What is the purpose of the second paragraph?" takes 5 seconds. A detail question also becomes quick, because you know which paragraph to search.

### Words that signal the passage structure
| Signal words | What they tell you |
|---|---|
| however, yet, but, still | the author is turning — the important point usually comes AFTER this word |
| because, since, as, due to | a reason — "why" questions are answered here |
| so, therefore, thus, as a result | a result or conclusion |
| for example, such as, consider | an example — it supports the point just before it |
| first, then, finally | a sequence or list |

### Question types you will meet
- **Main idea / title / purpose** — about the whole passage.
- **Detail** — "According to the passage…" — answer is written in one line.
- **Inference** — "It can be inferred…" — answer is one small step from a line.
- **Vocabulary in context** — meaning of a word *as used in the passage*.
- **Tone / attitude** — how the author feels.
- **Structure types** (this subtopic): statement combinations (I, II, III), paragraph purpose, "why does the author mention…", how the passage is organised, and "which question can be answered from the passage".

### Order of solving
Do the quick, local questions first: vocabulary (needs only one sentence), then detail, then inference, and main idea/tone last — by then you understand the passage best.

### Golden rules
- **Passage only.** If an option is true in real life but not in the passage, it is wrong.
- **Beware extreme words**: *always, never, only, all, completely*. Passages usually speak moderately.
- **Same words ≠ same meaning.** An option that copies passage words but changes their meaning is a trap.
- **Mark and move.** If one question is stuck for more than 40 seconds, mark it and come back.

### Time plan for 5 questions (about 6–7 minutes)
Read: 2 min → each question: 30–45 s → final check: 30 s.

### Quick revision
- Read passage first, questions next, then return to lines.
- Map each paragraph in a few words.
- "However/yet/but" = the key point follows.
- For statement-combination questions, judge each statement separately, then pick the matching option.
- For "why does the author mention X", ask what point X *supports*, not what X *is*.
- Never use outside knowledge; never choose an extreme option without extreme words in the passage.

patterns.name: Statement combination (Which of the statements I, II, III is/are true?)
patterns.howToSpot: The question lists two or three numbered statements and the options say 'Only I', 'Only I and III', 'All of these'.
patterns.logic:
1. Check statement I against the passage: True, False or Not stated.
2. Do the same for II and III, one at a time.
3. 'Not stated' counts as NOT true.
4. Pick the option that matches your T/F list exactly.

*Why it works:* judging one short statement is easier than comparing four long options. Once you know one statement is false, you can cut every option that contains it.

example.q:
Passage: "The pond was dug in 2015. It fills during the monsoon and supplies water to forty families till March."
Which is/are true? I. The pond fills in the monsoon. II. It supplies water all year. III. Forty families use it.
(a) Only I (b) Only I and III (c) Only II and III (d) All of these
example.solution: I is stated → True. II: water lasts only *till March* → False. III is stated → True. So the answer is **(b) Only I and III**.

patterns.name: Purpose or role of a paragraph
patterns.howToSpot: 'The second paragraph mainly…', 'What role does the last paragraph play?', 'The purpose of paragraph 3 is to…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Recall your paragraph map (3–5 words per paragraph).
2. Ask: does this paragraph give a problem, a cause, an example, a solution, or a contrast?
3. Choose the option that names that job for THIS paragraph — not the job of a neighbouring paragraph.

*Why it works:* wrong options usually describe a different paragraph correctly.

example.q:
Para 1 says city buses are always late. Para 2 says this is because roads are jammed by parked cars. Para 3 suggests paid parking. The second paragraph mainly:
(a) describes the problem (b) explains the cause of the problem (c) offers a solution (d) praises bus drivers
example.solution: Para 2 gives the *reason* buses are late (parked cars). Option (a) is para 1's job and (c) is para 3's job. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Why does the author mention X? (function of an example)
patterns.howToSpot: 'The author mentions … in order to…', 'Why does the author refer to…?', 'The example of … is given to show…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find X in the passage.
2. Read the sentence BEFORE X — it usually states the point X supports.
3. The answer names that point (to illustrate / to prove / to contrast), not a description of X itself.

*Why it works:* examples never stand alone; they exist to support a claim nearby.

example.q: "Small savings add up. A tea-seller who keeps aside ₹20 a day has over ₹7,000 at the end of a year." Why is the tea-seller mentioned?
example.solution: The sentence before says 'Small savings add up'. The tea-seller is an example that *illustrates how small daily savings become a large sum*. He is not mentioned to talk about tea or about his income level.

patterns.name: How is the passage organised? (structure)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following best describes the organisation/structure of the passage?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the paragraph map in order: e.g. *past → present advantage → obstacle*.
2. Read each option and check every part of it against your map, in the same order.
3. Reject options with even one wrong part (e.g. 'no solution is offered' when a solution is given).

example.q:
Para 1: a village had no doctor. Para 2: a mobile clinic started visiting weekly. Para 3: child illness fell sharply. Best description?
(a) A problem, a response, and its result (b) Two views compared (c) A theory rejected (d) A list of causes
example.solution: Map: problem → response (clinic) → result (less illness). Answer: **(a)**.

patterns.name: Which question can be answered from the passage?
patterns.howToSpot: 'The passage answers which of the following questions?', 'Which question can be answered using the information in the passage?'
patterns.logic:
1. For each option, look for the exact information needed (a number, a name, a reason).
2. If the passage gives only part of it, or nothing, reject it.
3. The correct option is usually a *why* or *how* whose answer is clearly written.

*Trap:* options asking for exact numbers, years or names that the passage never gives.

example.q: Passage: "The school started a kitchen garden so that children could eat fresh vegetables at lunch." Which question is answered? (a) How big is the garden? (b) Why did the school start a kitchen garden? (c) Who planted the first seed? (d) When was the school built?
example.solution: Only the reason is given ('so that children could eat fresh vegetables'). Answer: **(b)**.

subtopics.title: Main idea, central theme and best-title questions
subtopics.concept:
These questions ask what the passage as a whole says. The main idea is the claim the author keeps returning to; the title is that claim compressed into a phrase.

**Where the main idea lives:** in the opening paragraph (often the first or last sentence of it) and again, restated, in the closing lines. Middle paragraphs supply support — examples, data, objections — and are rarely the theme themselves.

**The whole-passage test.** A correct theme/title must:
- be *supported by every* paragraph (not just one example),
- be *covered by* the passage (not drag in outside ideas),
- be *no stronger* than what the author claims.

Run the three failure checks on every option: too narrow (one paragraph's detail), too broad (a general truth the passage never argues), too extreme (adds always/never or a stance the author does not take).

**Compression test for titles.** Summarise the passage to yourself in ten words, then pick the option closest to your summary — never start from the options.

| Option type | What it looks like | How to kill it |
|---|---|---|
| Out of scope | True in the real world, never said in the passage | Ask: where is this stated? If nowhere, reject |
| Too extreme | uses *always, never, only, must, completely* | Passages usually argue moderately; extremes overstate |
| Reversal | says the opposite of a stated line | Re-read the line the option is built on |
| Too narrow / too broad | covers one example, or drags in ideas beyond the passage | A title must cover the WHOLE passage, not one paragraph |
| Verbatim bait | copies a phrase but changes its use | Word-for-word options in inference questions are usually wrong |

**Example of scope:** a passage that discusses heat islands in cities mainly to argue that local design fixes exist → theme = "urban heat is a local design problem with local solutions". "Global warming is heating the planet" is too broad; "white roofs reflect sunlight" is too narrow; "cities will become uninhabitable" is too extreme.

tricks.title: First and last sentence sketch
tricks.body: Read only the opening and closing sentences of the passage, plus the first sentence of each middle paragraph. That skeleton usually states or implies the theme — build your ten-word summary from it before looking at options.

example.q: Opening: 'Critics announced the death of the public library... The prediction has aged badly.' Closing: '...one of the few public institutions succeeding in both worlds.'
example.solution: Skeleton says: libraries were written off, but they now serve wider social roles and deserve recognition → theme = libraries remain vital public institutions, not relics.

tricks.title: Count the mentions
tricks.body: The concept the author repeats in different words across paragraphs is the theme. If an option's core idea appears in only one paragraph, it is a detail, not the theme.

tricks.title: Title vs theme wording
tricks.body: Titles are noun phrases ('The quiet comeback of the public library'); theme options are full claims. Do not reject a title for lacking a verb — reject it for wrong scope.

mistakes: Picking a title that names only the first paragraph's example.
Choosing the broadest-sounding option; broadness without passage support is a trap, not a virtue.
Confusing the author's concluding suggestion with the theme — a suggestion supports the idea, it is not the whole idea.
Selecting an option because its words appear in the passage; theme options paraphrase, they rarely quote.
subtopics.notes:
### What is the main idea?
The **main idea** (also called the *central idea* or *theme*) is the one big point the whole passage makes. Every paragraph helps to support it. A **title** is the main idea squeezed into a short heading. The **purpose** is *why* the author wrote the passage — to inform, to argue, to warn, to encourage.

Everyday example: a friend talks for five minutes about late trains, crowded coaches and dirty platforms. The main idea is not "trains are late". It is "*the railway service in our town is poor*". Each complaint supports that one point.

### Where to find it
- The **first paragraph** usually introduces the topic or problem.
- The **last paragraph** usually gives the author's conclusion or suggestion.
- Middle paragraphs give reasons, examples and data.

So the main idea = **topic (from the start) + the author's point about it (often at the end)**.

### The three tests for a correct main-idea option
1. **Covers the whole passage** — not just one paragraph or one example. (*Too narrow* = wrong.)
2. **Stays inside the passage** — does not add ideas the passage never discussed. (*Too broad* = wrong.)
3. **Matches the author's strength** — does not say *always, only, never* when the author was moderate. (*Too extreme* = wrong.)

### Worked example
Passage (short): *"Many old stepwells lie full of garbage. Yet a few towns that cleaned them found they still collect rainwater and raise groundwater. Reviving them costs little."*
- "Stepwells are full of garbage" → too narrow (only first line).
- "India faces a water crisis" → too broad (the passage talks only about stepwells).
- "Only stepwells can solve water shortage" → too extreme.
- "**Cleaning old stepwells is a cheap way to improve water supply**" → correct: covers all lines.

### Title questions
A good title is short, covers the whole passage and often shows both sides if the passage has both. Titles with a colon ("Gig Work: Freedom with a Price") are common right answers because they hold two halves of the idea.

**Title trap:** a catchy option that names only the *first example*. If the passage starts with a farmer's story but is really about water policy, "A Farmer's Story" is too narrow.

### Purpose questions
Look at the verbs the author uses:
| Author mainly… | Purpose word |
|---|---|
| gives facts, explains how something works | to inform / to explain |
| gives reasons for one side, says "should/must" | to argue / to persuade |
| points out a danger | to warn |
| praises something and asks readers to do it | to encourage |
| points out faults | to criticise |

If the passage is a neutral explanation, "to criticise" or "to persuade" is wrong even if the topic is serious.

### Paragraph main point
Some questions ask the main point of just one paragraph. Apply the same three tests, but to that paragraph only. Its first sentence (the *topic sentence*) usually states the point.

### Method (30–40 seconds)
1. Before looking at options, say the main idea in about ten words.
2. Remove options that are too narrow, too broad, or too extreme.
3. Between two survivors, pick the one that includes the author's conclusion.

### Quick revision
- Main idea = topic + author's point about it.
- Check first and last paragraphs first.
- Three killers: too narrow, too broad, too extreme.
- Title = whole passage in a few words; colon titles often fit two-sided passages.
- Purpose = why it was written: inform, argue, warn, encourage, criticise.
- Make your own summary before reading options.

patterns.name: Central idea / main theme of the passage
patterns.howToSpot: 'The central idea/main theme of the passage is…', 'The passage is primarily concerned with…', 'Which option sums up the passage?'
patterns.logic:
1. Say the topic (from para 1) + the author's point (usually in the last para) in one line.
2. Cut options that cover only one paragraph (too narrow).
3. Cut options that talk about a bigger subject than the passage (too broad).
4. Cut options with *only/always/never* the author did not use (too extreme).

*Why it works:* the main idea must be supported by every paragraph, so partial or inflated options fail.

example.q:
"Many families now buy bottled water. Yet a simple home filter gives safe water at a tenth of the cost, and it creates no plastic waste." The central idea is:
(a) Bottled water is unsafe (b) Home filters are a cheaper, cleaner alternative to bottled water (c) Plastic waste is rising in India (d) All families should stop drinking water from taps
example.solution: Topic: bottled water. Author's point: a home filter is cheaper and creates no plastic. (a) is never said; (c) is too broad; (d) is extreme and unrelated. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Most suitable title
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is the most appropriate/suitable title for the passage?'
patterns.logic:
1. Build your ten-word summary first.
2. Reject titles that name only an example from one paragraph.
3. Reject dramatic titles that go beyond the author (e.g. 'The End of…', 'The Only Way…').
4. Prefer the title that covers both the problem and the author's answer if the passage has both.

example.q:
A passage describes how a village built check dams, how its wells refilled and how farmers now grow two crops. Best title?
(a) Check Dams Bring a Village Back to Life (b) How to Build a Wall (c) Farming in India (d) The Monsoon Always Fails
example.solution: (b) misses the effect, (c) is too broad, (d) is extreme and not discussed. (a) covers the action and the result. Answer: **(a)**.

patterns.name: Author's primary purpose
patterns.howToSpot: 'The author's main purpose is to…', 'The passage has been written mainly to…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Notice the author's verbs: *explains* (inform), *should/must* (argue), *danger/risk* (warn), *praises + asks readers* (encourage).
2. Match the purpose to the WHOLE passage, not to one sentence.
3. Reject purposes that are too strong (demand, prove) if the author only suggests.

example.q:
"Fifteen minutes of reading to a child each evening builds vocabulary. It needs no costly books — a folk tale works as well. Busy parents can surely spare this time." The author's purpose is to:
(a) criticise schools (b) encourage parents to read or tell stories to children daily (c) sell children's books (d) compare folk tales
example.solution: The author explains a benefit and then urges parents ('can surely spare this time'). Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Main point of one paragraph / best summary
patterns.howToSpot: 'The second paragraph is mainly about…', 'What is the main point of the last paragraph?', 'Which option best summarises…'
patterns.logic:
1. Read the first sentence of that paragraph (the topic sentence).
2. Check that the option fits every sentence in that paragraph.
3. Reject options that describe another paragraph.

example.q:
Para 2: "Discarded phones add to e-waste. Workers burn wires to get copper and breathe the fumes. New phones need fresh metals and energy." Para 2 is mainly about:
(a) new phone features (b) the hidden costs of throwing gadgets away (c) the price of copper (d) government rules on repair
example.solution: Every sentence names a cost of discarding (waste, fumes, fresh resources). Answer: **(b)**.

subtopics.title: Factual detail questions ('According to the passage…')
subtopics.concept:
These questions ask what the passage *says*, line by line. The answer is written in the passage — but the options paraphrase it, and the wrong options are engineered around it.

**Method: locate → read around → paraphrase-match.**
1. Pull the distinctive keyword from the question (a proper noun, a number, an unusual noun like *pensions* or *tin roofs*).
2. Find it in the passage; read the sentence before and after — the answer often sits just outside the keyword's own line.
3. State the answer to yourself in your own words, then choose the option that matches your sentence. Never compare options to the passage directly; compare them to your paraphrase.

**The three wrong options in detail questions:**
- **Not stated:** plausible, even true in the world, but the passage never says it.
- **Reversed:** right topic, opposite direction — often built by flipping one word (*most* ↔ *least*, *can* ↔ *cannot*).
- **Wrong scope:** takes a detail from a different paragraph and attaches it here.

**Comparatives, numbers and qualifiers deserve double attention.** If the passage says "night-time heat is *particularly* dangerous", an option that drops "particularly" and says heat is dangerous is weaker than the passage allows — and an option saying "day-time heat is the real danger" is reversed.

**"Which of the following is NOT true" variants:** mark each option TRUE or FALSE against a line; the odd one out is the answer. Two options will usually share one sentence, which helps you locate the region fast.

tricks.title: Paraphrase before you look
tricks.body: After locating the line, cover the options, answer aloud in your own words, then uncover. This one habit defeats most engineered wrong options.

example.q: 'Why is night-time heat more dangerous than day heat?' (from a passage on heat islands)
example.solution: Your paraphrase: body repairs itself during sleep, so hot nights harm health. Now match — any option about air conditioners or daytime labour is off-line.

tricks.title: Reversal scan
tricks.body: Before marking a detail option, check its direction words: only/always/all, may/often/some, can/cannot. Wrong options flip these while keeping the same topic words.

tricks.title: Option pairing
tricks.body: When two options say the same thing in different words, both are wrong — a fact has one meaning. Kill the pair, then judge the remaining two.

mistakes: Stopping at the line containing the keyword; the answer may be in the following sentence.
Choosing an option because it sounds authoritative ('studies show…') though the passage cites no such study.
Missing 'EXCEPT/NOT' in the question stem and marking the true statement instead.
Ignoring qualifiers like 'mainly', 'only', 'some' — detail questions turn on exactly these words.
subtopics.notes:
### What is a detail question?
A detail (or *factual*) question asks about something that is **written directly** in the passage: a fact, a reason, a number, a name, a feature. The stem often begins *"According to the passage…"* or *"The passage states that…"*.

These are the easiest marks in RC — but only if you go back and read the line. Memory is not enough, because the options are built to *almost* match the passage.

### Method: Locate → Read around → Say it → Match
1. **Locate.** Pick a keyword from the question — a name, number or unusual word (*stepwell, fat content, ten days*). Find it in the passage.
2. **Read around.** Read that sentence plus one before and one after. Answers often sit in the next sentence.
3. **Say it.** Put the answer in your own words before looking at the options.
4. **Match.** Choose the option that means the same as your words (options usually *paraphrase* — use different words with the same meaning).

### How wrong options are made
| Trap | Example (passage says "Most varieties need little water") |
|---|---|
| **Reversal** — opposite meaning | "Millets need a lot of water" |
| **Extreme** — changes *most* to *all* | "All millets need no water at all" |
| **Not stated** — sounds true, never said | "Millets are grown mainly in Punjab" |
| **Wrong part** — true detail from another paragraph, wrong for this question | a reason given for a different fact |

### Watch the small words (qualifiers)
*some / many / most / all*, *often / always*, *may / will*, *more / less*, *only*. One changed qualifier makes an option wrong.
- Passage: "Rich merchants and queens paid for **the finest** of them."
- Option: "**All** stepwells were paid for by queens." → wrong (two changes: *all* and *only queens*).

### Reason questions ("Why…?")
Look for **because, since, as, so that, due to, the reason is**. The answer is the clause after these words.
- Passage: "Less milk turned sour **because** it was cooled at once."
- Q: Why did less milk turn sour? → "It was cooled immediately."

### NOT / EXCEPT questions
"Which of the following is NOT mentioned…" or "…all of the following EXCEPT".
1. Circle NOT/EXCEPT so you do not forget it.
2. Tick each option you can find in the passage.
3. The one option you **cannot** find (or that is contradicted) is the answer.
Three options usually come from the same sentence or list — find that list and it is quick.

### Numbers and comparisons
If the passage gives numbers ("twelve households… over two hundred within four years"), check every number in the option. A common trap swaps the *before* and *after* figures.

### Quick revision
- Detail answers are WRITTEN in the passage — always go back to the line.
- Use a keyword to locate; read one sentence before and after.
- Answer in your own words first, then match the paraphrase.
- Traps: reversal, extreme, not stated, wrong paragraph.
- "Why" → look for *because / since / so that*.
- NOT/EXCEPT → tick the three that are present; the leftover is the answer.
- Check qualifiers and numbers word by word.

patterns.name: Direct detail ('According to the passage…')
patterns.howToSpot: The stem asks what, when, how often, or what happened, usually with 'according to the passage'.
patterns.logic:
1. Take the keyword from the question and find it.
2. Read that sentence and the next one.
3. Say the answer in your words, then pick the matching paraphrase.
4. Double-check qualifiers (some/most/all).

example.q: "The library opens at 9 a.m. on weekdays and at noon on Sundays." According to the passage, when does the library open on Sundays?
example.solution: Keyword *Sundays* → 'at noon on Sundays'. Answer: **at 12 noon**.

patterns.name: Reason / cause detail ('Why…?')
patterns.howToSpot: 'Why did…?', 'What was the reason for…?', 'According to the passage, … because…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the event the question names.
2. Look for *because, since, as, so that, due to* near it.
3. The clause after that word is the answer. Match it with the option that gives the SAME reason, not a related fact.

example.q: "Travellers rested in the stepwell at noon because the air near the water stayed cool." Why did travellers rest there?
example.solution: The clause after *because*: the air near the water stayed cool. Answer: **because it was cool near the water**.

patterns.name: NOT mentioned / EXCEPT
patterns.howToSpot: The stem contains NOT or EXCEPT (often in capitals).
patterns.logic:
1. Circle NOT/EXCEPT.
2. Find the list or sentence the options come from.
3. Tick each option present in the passage.
4. The one left (not present or contradicted) is the answer.

example.q: "The kit contains a torch, a whistle and a first-aid box." Which is NOT in the kit? (a) torch (b) whistle (c) rope (d) first-aid box
example.solution: Torch, whistle and first-aid box are listed. Rope is not. Answer: **(c) rope**.

patterns.name: Which statement is true / correct? (qualifiers and numbers)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which of the following is true/correct according to the passage?' with four full-sentence options.
patterns.logic:
1. Test each option against its line.
2. Look hard at qualifiers (*all, only, every, most*) and numbers.
3. An option with one wrong word is fully wrong.

*Why it works:* setters make three options false by changing one small word each.

example.q: "The club began with 12 members and had 200 members four years later." Which is true? (a) It began with 200 members (b) It grew from 12 to 200 members in four years (c) It lost members (d) It has 12 members now
example.solution: (a) swaps the numbers, (c) reverses, (d) uses the old figure. Answer: **(b)**.

subtopics.title: Inference and extrapolation questions
subtopics.concept:
An inference is something the passage *strongly implies* without stating. The line between detail and inference: if the option can be pointed to as a sentence, it is a detail; if it is the unavoidable next step of a stated sentence, it is an inference.

**The must-be-true test.** Ask: if this option were false, would the passage contradict itself? For a valid inference, yes. If the passage could still stand with the option false, the option goes too far.

**Distance control.** The correct inference sits one small step from the text:
- passage: "she cannot afford the electricity that cooling demands" → inference: cooling appliances are of limited use to the poorest residents (small step ✔);
- "her city will ban air conditioners" (large step ✘);
- "she cannot afford electricity" verbatim (that is a detail, not an inference ✘ for inference questions).

**Outside knowledge is banned.** If an inference needs a fact you happen to know — a court ruling, a statistic — it is wrong for this exam. The passage is the only permitted world.

| Option type | What it looks like | How to kill it |
|---|---|---|
| Out of scope | True in the real world, never said in the passage | Ask: where is this stated? If nowhere, reject |
| Too extreme | uses *always, never, only, must, completely* | Passages usually argue moderately; extremes overstate |
| Reversal | says the opposite of a stated line | Re-read the line the option is built on |
| Too narrow / too broad | covers one example, or drags in ideas beyond the passage | A title must cover the WHOLE passage, not one paragraph |
| Verbatim bait | copies a phrase but changes its use | Word-for-word options in inference questions are usually wrong |

**Author-intent variants** ("Why does the author mention Ahmedabad's plan?"): the answer is the point of the surrounding argument — here, that heat action is affordable and already working. Wrong options describe what the example *literally is* rather than what it *does*.

tricks.title: One-step rule
tricks.body: Correct inference = stated idea + one logical step. If you need two steps, extra facts, or a change of scale (one city → all countries), reject it.

example.q: Passage: 'A workforce that cannot plan a month ahead cannot borrow, train or save with confidence.'
example.solution: One step: income insecurity itself blocks long-term commitments. Two steps: gig work will soon be banned (needs outside assumption) ✘.

tricks.title: Verbatim is a verdict
tricks.body: In an inference question, an option that repeats passage wording without adding the step is wrong by definition. Cross it out first.

tricks.title: Extremity filter
tricks.body: Inferences with *only, never, must, inevitably* are almost always one step too far. Moderate options (*may, tends to, is likely*) fit the must-be-true test better.

mistakes: Importing real-world facts to justify an option the passage never supports.
Treating a copied line as an inference (it is a detail).
Inferring the author's personal life or politics from a neutral informational passage.
Choosing an inference so weak it could follow from any passage — it must follow from *this* one.
subtopics.notes:
### What is an inference?
To **infer** means to reach a conclusion from clues. The passage does not say it in words, but it is **clearly suggested**. If a detail is written on the page, an inference is *one small step* beyond the page.

Everyday example: your friend comes in with a wet umbrella and wet shoes. Nobody told you, but you can **infer** that it is raining outside. You cannot infer that "it will rain all week" — that is too big a step.

### Detail vs inference vs wrong
Passage: *"Harish's free solar pump let him water his fields for longer than the crop needed. Two years later, his borewell water had dropped."*
| Option | Type |
|---|---|
| "Harish watered his fields for longer than needed." | detail (written) |
| "Free power led Harish to over-use groundwater." | **inference** (one step) ✔ |
| "Solar pumps always destroy groundwater." | too big a step ✘ |
| "Harish will sell his land." | no support ✘ |

### The must-be-true test
For each option ask: *"If this were false, would the passage stop making sense?"*
- If yes → strong inference, likely correct.
- If the passage could still be true → the option is only a guess. Reject it.

### Types of inference questions
1. **"It can be inferred…" / "The passage suggests…"** — the general type.
2. **Implied meaning of a line** — "What does the author mean by '…'?" The answer explains the idea behind the words, often a figure of speech.
3. **Assumption** — something the author *takes for granted* without saying it. Without it, the argument would not work.
   - Argument: "Caterers cook extra food because running short is a disgrace."
   - Assumption: *leftover food is less embarrassing than running out*.
4. **Prediction / application** — "What is most likely to happen if…?" or "Which situation is most similar to…?" Use the passage's own logic on the new case.

### How to handle an assumption question
1. Find the conclusion (what the author wants you to accept).
2. Find the reason given.
3. Ask: what hidden link joins the reason to the conclusion? That link is the assumption.
4. Check: if the assumption were false, the conclusion would collapse.

### How to handle a prediction / application question
1. Say the passage's rule in simple words: *"extra sunshine now earns money instead of pumping more water."*
2. Apply that rule to the new situation.
3. Pick the option that follows the SAME rule. Reject options that need new information.

### Traps
- **Copied line**: an option that repeats a sentence word for word is a detail, not an inference. For "infer" questions, it is usually not the best answer.
- **Outside knowledge**: "Solar panels last 25 years" may be true, but if the passage does not support it, it is wrong.
- **Too extreme**: *all, always, never, must, completely*.
- **Added motive**: an option that says someone did something "deliberately" or "to hurt" when the passage gives no motive.

### Quick revision
- Inference = one small step from a line, never a big leap.
- Use the must-be-true test.
- Implied meaning → explain the idea behind the words.
- Assumption → hidden link between reason and conclusion.
- Prediction/application → apply the passage's rule to the new case.
- Reject: word-for-word copies, outside facts, extreme words, invented motives.

patterns.name: 'It can be inferred from the passage that…'
patterns.howToSpot: Stem uses infer, imply, suggest, 'most probably', or 'it can be concluded'.
patterns.logic:
1. Find the line the question is about.
2. Take ONE logical step from that line.
3. Apply the must-be-true test to each option.
4. Reject copies, extremes, and outside facts.

example.q:
"The shop is crowded every morning since the government moved its forms online." What can be inferred?
(a) Many people need help filling online forms (b) The government has closed all offices (c) The shop sells food (d) People dislike computers
example.solution: Crowd began when forms went online → people come for help with online forms. (b) is extreme, (c) unsupported, (d) contradicts (they come to use computers). Answer: **(a)**.

patterns.name: Implied meaning of a quoted line
patterns.howToSpot: 'What does the author mean by…?', 'The statement "…" implies that…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the quoted line and the sentence around it.
2. Ask what idea the line expresses (often figurative).
3. Choose the option that explains the idea, not one that reads the words literally.

example.q: "Earlier, extra sunshine meant extra pumping. Now it means extra money." What is implied?
example.solution: Earlier, spare solar power was used to pump more water; now the farmer sells spare power. So: **surplus power now earns money instead of being spent on pumping**.

patterns.name: Assumption behind a statement
patterns.howToSpot: 'The author assumes that…', 'The statement is based on the assumption that…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Separate reason and conclusion.
2. Find the unstated link that makes the reason lead to the conclusion.
3. Negate the option: if the argument breaks, it is the assumption.

example.q: "The road will reduce travel time, so traders will earn more." What is assumed?
example.solution: Link needed: saving travel time helps traders earn more (for example, they can sell more or reach markets sooner). If time saved did not matter to earnings, the conclusion would fail. Answer: **traders' earnings depend partly on travel time**.

patterns.name: Prediction or application (most likely / most similar)
patterns.howToSpot: 'If … happens, which is most likely?', 'Which of the following situations is most similar to…?'
patterns.logic:
1. Write the passage's rule in one line.
2. Apply it to the new case.
3. The answer follows the same rule; reject options that need extra facts or go to extremes.

example.q: Passage: volunteers collect untouched wedding food and give it to shelters. Most similar: (a) a shop raising prices (b) a bakery giving unsold bread to an orphanage (c) a family cooking less (d) a hotel adding new dishes
example.solution: Rule: surplus food is collected and given to people in need. Only (b) follows it. Answer: **(b)**.

subtopics.title: Vocabulary in context (replace-the-word / meaning questions)
subtopics.concept:
SSC RC asks the meaning of a word **as used in the passage** — which can differ from the word's common meaning. The question is local: only one sentence matters.

**The plug-in test (works on every such question):**
1. Read the sentence containing the word.
2. Substitute each option into that sentence.
3. Keep the sentence's meaning, grammar and tone intact — that option is the answer. Words are rarely synonymous in isolation; they are synonymous *in this sentence*.

**Guard the part of speech.** *Models* as a noun (examples to copy) and as a verb (poses as) fit different blanks. Identify the role of the word in its sentence before plugging in.

**Expect the shift.** Passage setters choose words with a double life:
- *cushions* an illness = protects against its impact (not bedroom cushions);
- *dipped* = declined briefly (not dipped into water);
- *interest* in banking = a charge; *interest* in reading = curiosity.
If one option matches the word's *dictionary* meaning and another matches the *sentence*, the sentence wins.

**Phrase-in-context variants** ("turn bedrooms into ovens", "marked for closure"): treat the phrase as one unit; its meaning is figurative or idiomatic within the passage. Literal word-by-word options are the bait.

**Antonym-in-context variants** ask which word is *opposite* to the passage word — still test the sentence, then flip the meaning once. Do not flip twice.

tricks.title: Own-words first
tricks.body: Cover the options, replace the word with your own simple word, then find the option matching YOUR word. This kills the dictionary-meaning bait.

example.q: '...no paid leave cushions an illness.' What does *cushions* mean here?
example.solution: Own word: *softens/protects against*. Match options: 'protects from the effects of' ✔; 'provides comfort in the home' ✘ (dictionary bait).

tricks.title: Tone match
tricks.body: The substitute must keep the sentence's attitude. In a critical sentence, choose the critical option; a neutral synonym that drains the criticism is wrong.

tricks.title: Two-line rule for phrases
tricks.body: For phrase-meaning questions, read one line before and after: figurative phrases get their meaning from the surrounding argument, not from the words themselves.

mistakes: Picking the option with the word's most common meaning although the sentence demands another sense.
Changing the part of speech while plugging in (noun option in a verb slot).
Choosing an opposite for an antonym question because it merely sounds negative.
Reading five lines around the word; context questions need the sentence, at most the sentence plus its neighbour.
subtopics.notes:
### What is vocabulary in context?
These questions give a word or phrase **from the passage** and ask its meaning *as used in the passage*. Many English words have more than one meaning. The passage decides which meaning is right.

Example: the word **bank**.
- *She deposited money in the bank.* → a place for money.
- *They sat on the bank of the river.* → the side of a river.
Both meanings are correct English, but only one fits each sentence.

### The plug-in test (use it every time)
1. Read the full sentence that contains the word.
2. Cover the word and think of your own simple word that fits.
3. Put each option in place of the word.
4. The right option keeps the sentence's meaning, grammar and tone.

Worked example: *"Buyers from three districts **haggled** cheerfully over prices."*
- Your own word: *bargained*.
- "quarrelled violently" — does not fit *cheerfully*. ✘
- "bargained" — fits perfectly. ✔

### Question types
1. **Synonym in context** — closest meaning.
2. **Antonym in context** — most nearly opposite. First find the meaning in the sentence, then take its opposite **once**.
   - *"It was a **modest** victory"* → modest = small → opposite = huge/sweeping. Not "proud" (that is the opposite of the *other* meaning of modest, "humble").
3. **Phrase or idiom meaning** — e.g. *did not take it lying down* = refused to accept without a fight; *cut corners* = skipped necessary steps to save time or money. Treat the phrase as one unit.
4. **Multiple-meaning word** — the setter picks a word whose common meaning is a trap: *shelved* (postponed, not put on a shelf), *craft* (skill, not a boat), *toll* (loss/damage, not a road tax).

### Keep the part of speech
If the word is a verb in the passage, the answer must work as a verb in that sentence. *"The board **shelved** the plan"* — *shelved* is a past-tense verb, so "postponed" fits; "a shelf" (noun) cannot.

### Watch the tone
Positive, negative or neutral? *"The traders **celebrated**"* is positive; an option like "mourned" breaks the tone even if you are unsure of meanings.

### Common multiple-meaning words in exam passages
| Word | Everyday meaning | Other meaning often used |
|---|---|---|
| shelve | put on a shelf | postpone, set aside |
| craft | handmade object / boat | skill, profession |
| toll | road tax | damage, loss of life |
| frank | — | honest, open |
| check | examine | stop, control ("check the spread") |
| sound | noise | healthy, reliable ("sound advice") |
| grave | burial place | serious ("a grave mistake") |
| novel | story book | new, original ("a novel idea") |
| bear | animal | tolerate / carry |
| fine | good | penalty; very thin |

### Speed tip
Vocabulary questions need only one sentence. Do them **first** in the RC set — 20 seconds each.

### Quick revision
- Meaning comes from the sentence, not from the dictionary's first meaning.
- Plug-in test: your own word first, then options.
- Antonym: find meaning in context, then flip once.
- Idioms/phrases: read as one unit; literal options are traps.
- Keep part of speech and tone.
- Do vocab questions first.

patterns.name: Synonym in context (closest meaning)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which word is closest in meaning to X as used in the passage?', 'X most nearly means…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Read the sentence with the word.
2. Think of your own replacement word.
3. Plug in each option; keep meaning, grammar and tone.
4. Choose the option that works in the sentence, even if another option is a more common meaning.

example.q: "When the board finally **unveiled** its plan for a mall…" Closest meaning: (a) hid (b) made public (c) cancelled (d) painted
example.solution: The board showed the plan to the public for the first time. Own word: *announced*. Answer: **(b) made public**.

patterns.name: Antonym in context (most nearly opposite)
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which word is most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning to X as used in the passage?'
patterns.logic:
1. Find the word's meaning in the sentence first.
2. Take the opposite of THAT meaning — only once.
3. Reject options that are synonyms (setters include one) or opposites of a different meaning.

example.q: "Scientists are **frank** about the limits of their craft." Opposite: (a) honest (b) evasive (c) open (d) direct
example.solution: Frank = honest and open. Opposite = avoiding the truth. (a), (c), (d) are synonyms. Answer: **(b) evasive**.

patterns.name: Meaning of a phrase or idiom in the passage
patterns.howToSpot: A quoted phrase: 'The phrase "…" means…', 'What does the author mean by "…"?'
patterns.logic:
1. Treat the phrase as one unit.
2. Use the sentence before and after to see what happened.
3. Reject literal word-by-word options.

example.q: "Officials under pressure are tempted to **cut corners**." Meaning?
example.solution: Context: codes cost money; officials want quick results. So *cut corners* = **save time or money by skipping necessary steps** — not literally cutting anything.

patterns.name: Multiple-meaning word (which sense is used?)
patterns.howToSpot: A familiar word whose everyday meaning is an option (shelved, craft, toll, check, sound).
patterns.logic:
1. Assume the common meaning is a trap.
2. Plug in each meaning; only one keeps the sentence sensible.
3. Confirm part of speech.

example.q: "The board **shelved** the plan and repaired the roof instead." Shelved means: (a) arranged on shelves (b) put aside (c) sold (d) announced
example.solution: A plan cannot be placed on a shelf; the board dropped it for now. Answer: **(b) put aside**.

subtopics.title: Tone, attitude and author's-opinion questions
subtopics.concept:
Tone questions ask *how* the author speaks, not *what* he says. Tone lives in adjectives, adverbs and contrasts — not in the facts themselves.

| Tone | Signature words | Example signal |
|---|---|---|
| Neutral / informative | states facts, figures, findings | no praise or blame anywhere |
| Critical | flaws, fails to, merely, despite promises | points out problems repeatedly |
| Optimistic / appreciative | promising, remarkably, has become a model | highlights success and progress |
| Sceptical / cautionary | claimed, supposedly, yet, the deeper cost | accepts a claim, then questions it |
| Balanced / analytical | however, on the other hand, both | gives two sides, then weighs them |

**How to read for tone in one pass:** watch the author's evaluations. "has become a model studied by other countries" = approval. "merely shifts risk onto workers" = criticism. "The prediction has aged badly" = gentle mockery of critics. Underline one evaluative phrase per paragraph; the pattern across paragraphs is the tone.

**Author's-opinion questions** ("The author would agree with which of these?") obey the same rules as inference, with one addition — the opinion must match the author's *degree* of commitment. Authors of SSC passages usually take measured positions: they accept problems and propose workable fixes. Options claiming the author is desperate, euphoric, or completely dismissive of something almost never fit.

**Neutral passages exist.** Science and report-style passages carry no stance; the correct tone is *informative/neutral/analytical*, and options like *sarcastic, pessimistic, passionate* are wrong even when the topic sounds alarming. Do not confuse the seriousness of a subject with the mood of the writer.

**Attitude toward a specific thing** ("attitude of the author towards gig platforms"): collect every line touching that thing, note the verbs used with it (*celebrate, warn, can be applied now*), and summarise: the author is critical of the rules but not of flexibility itself. One-sided options (fully supportive / fully hostile) fail.

tricks.title: Adjective audit
tricks.body: Sweep the passage for adjectives and adverbs with feeling (quietly, badly, remarkable, merely, confident). Three of them in the same direction fix the tone.

example.q: Passage words: 'quietly getting hotter', 'turn bedrooms into ovens', 'plan itself out of one'.
example.solution: Concerned but hopeful: the problem is real and the closing line offers a way out → tone = concerned/optimistic, not alarmed or dismissive.

tricks.title: However counts double
tricks.body: The clause after *but/however/yet* carries the author's real position; the clause before it is the position being set aside. Tone and opinion questions key off the second half.

tricks.title: Degree matching
tricks.body: Match intensity, not just direction: 'sceptical' ≠ 'hostile', 'cautiously optimistic' ≠ 'confident'. Pick the option at the same temperature as the passage.

mistakes: Calling a fact-heavy passage 'sarcastic' because its subject is unpleasant.
Reading the tone of people *quoted* in the passage as the author's own tone.
Choosing an extreme tone word (outraged, euphoric) when the passage argues moderately.
Forgetting that a 'balanced/analytical' option is often correct when the author gives both sides.
subtopics.notes:
### What is tone?
**Tone** is the author's feeling or manner in writing — the *voice* behind the words. The same fact can be written in different tones:
- Neutral: "The lake has become polluted."
- Critical: "Despite crores spent on brochures, the lake is still a sewer."
- Hopeful: "With a few drains, the lake can be clean again."

**Attitude** is the author's feeling towards one particular thing in the passage (a plan, a group, an idea).

### Where tone hides
Tone is carried by **describing words** (adjectives and adverbs) and by **contrast words**.
- *glossy brochures, grand plan, the cameras leave* → mocking the show.
- *"Surely a city that can spend crores on brochures can find money for a drain"* → sarcasm (saying something to point out a failure).
- *however, yet, but* → the part after it shows what the author really thinks.

### Common tone words and their meanings
| Tone word | Meaning | Sign in the passage |
|---|---|---|
| informative / objective / neutral | only gives facts | no praise, no blame |
| analytical | examines causes and effects | "because", "as a result", weighs points |
| critical | points out faults | *fails, merely, despite promises* |
| sarcastic / ironic | mocks by saying the opposite or exaggerating | *Surely…, what a grand plan* |
| appreciative / laudatory | praises | *remarkable, a model, succeeded* |
| optimistic / hopeful | expects good results | *can, will improve, promising* |
| pessimistic | expects bad results | *hopeless, bound to fail* |
| balanced | gives both sides fairly | *neither… nor, on one hand… on the other* |
| nostalgic | fondly remembers the past | *those were the days* |
| cautionary | warns | *risk, danger, before we…* |
| indifferent | does not care | rarely correct — authors write because they care |

### Method
1. Underline one evaluative phrase in each paragraph.
2. Is it positive, negative, or neutral? How strong?
3. Check the **last sentence** — it usually shows the final attitude.
4. Pick the tone word that matches both *direction* (positive/negative) and *strength* (mild/strong).

### Degree matters
If the author says online classes are "neither the saviour nor the failure" — the tone is **balanced**, not "angry" and not "celebratory". Extreme tone words (*furious, euphoric, hostile*) are usually wrong in exam passages.

### Serious topic ≠ emotional tone
A science passage about germs or earthquakes is still **informative** if it just explains. Do not call it "alarmed" because the subject is scary.

### "Author would agree" questions
These are inference questions about the author's opinion. The correct option matches what the author says **and** how strongly. If the author wants "sewage stopped before ceremonies", he would agree that *stopping sewage matters more than publicity* — not that "the lake can never be cleaned".

### "The passage is most likely taken from…"
Match style to the type of text:
- facts + explanations, no opinion → science book / textbook / encyclopaedia
- opinion on a current issue with suggestions → newspaper editorial / opinion piece
- personal feelings in first person, dates → diary / memoir
- story with characters and dialogue → short story
- selling words (best, buy now) → advertisement

### Quick revision
- Tone = author's voice; attitude = feeling towards one thing.
- Look at adjectives, adverbs and what comes after *however/yet/but*.
- Match direction AND degree; avoid extreme tone words.
- Serious subject can still have a neutral tone.
- Quoted people's feelings are not the author's tone.
- Source questions: match the writing style to the type of text.

patterns.name: Tone of the passage
patterns.howToSpot: 'The tone of the passage is…', 'Which word best describes the author's tone?'
patterns.logic:
1. Collect the evaluative words (adjectives, adverbs, 'surely', 'merely').
2. Decide direction (positive / negative / neutral) and strength.
3. Confirm with the closing sentence.
4. Reject extremes and tone words that fit only one line.

example.q: "The new bridge, built in record time and under budget, has cut the travel time of thousands of commuters." Tone: (a) critical (b) appreciative (c) sarcastic (d) indifferent
example.solution: 'Record time', 'under budget', 'cut travel time' are praise. No mockery. Answer: **(b) appreciative**.

patterns.name: Author's attitude towards a specific thing
patterns.howToSpot: 'The author's attitude towards X is…', 'How does the author view…?'
patterns.logic:
1. Find every line that mentions X.
2. Note the words used with X (praise, doubt, blame).
3. Summarise in one phrase and match; reject one-sided options if the author gives both sides.

example.q: "Online classes were a lifeline for children with laptops, and a blank screen for children without them." Attitude towards online classes?
example.solution: Positive for some, useless for others → the author sees them as **useful but dependent on access** — neither fully good nor fully bad.

patterns.name: Author would agree / disagree with…
patterns.howToSpot: 'With which statement would the author most likely agree?'
patterns.logic:
1. Recall the author's main opinion (usually in the last lines).
2. Pick the option that follows from it at the same strength.
3. Reject options that are extreme, opposite, or about something the author never discussed.

example.q:
Author: "Brochures are printed every year, but the sewage pipes are never diverted." The author would agree that:
(a) brochures clean lakes (b) fixing sewage matters more than publicity (c) the lake cannot be saved (d) sewage is harmless
example.solution: The author criticises show without action. Answer: **(b)**.

patterns.name: Type or source of the passage
patterns.howToSpot: 'The passage is most likely taken from…', 'The passage is an example of…'.
patterns.logic:
1. Is it facts only (textbook), opinion with suggestions (editorial), a story (fiction), personal feelings (diary), or selling (advertisement)?
2. Match that style with the option.

example.q: "Honey resists decay because it has little water, is slightly acidic and contains an enzyme that produces hydrogen peroxide." Source?
example.solution: Only facts and explanation, no opinion or selling → **a science book or article**.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Central theme / main idea of the passage
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem says 'the central idea/main theme of the passage', 'the passage is primarily concerned with' or 'which option sums up the passage'. Almost every RC set has one such question.
pyqPatterns.approach: Before reading the options, say the topic (from the first paragraph) and the author's point (usually in the last lines) in about ten words. Then remove options that cover only one paragraph, options that talk about a bigger subject, and options with extreme words like only/always.

example.q: A passage says people throw away gadgets because repair is hard, that this creates e-waste, and that new rules on spare parts can make repair possible again. Central idea?
example.solution: Hard-to-repair products create hidden waste, and rules that make repair possible can reduce it. Options about only e-waste workers or only solar power are too narrow or off-topic.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem asks for 'the most appropriate/suitable title'. Options are short headings.
pyqPatterns.approach: A title is the main idea in a few words. It must cover every paragraph. Reject titles built on the first example, dramatic titles the author would not use, and titles about a bigger subject. Two-part titles with a colon often fit passages that give a problem and a solution.

example.q: A passage: city footpaths are broken, this is dangerous and adds to traffic, and good footpaths are cheap. Best title?
example.solution: 'Walking Matters: Why Cities Must Fix Their Footpaths' — covers problem and demand. 'A History of Road Accidents' is too broad.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem asks what, when, how often or why something happened, usually beginning 'According to the passage'. The answer is written in one or two lines.
pyqPatterns.approach: Take a keyword from the question, find it in the passage and read the sentence before and after. Say the answer in your own words, then match the option that paraphrases it. Check small words like all/most/only and every number.

example.q: Passage: 'Money was paid every ten days, directly into bank accounts.' The old trader 'delayed payment for weeks'. How often did the cooperative pay?
example.solution: Every ten days. 'After several weeks' describes the old trader — a trap from another line.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem contains NOT or EXCEPT, often in capital letters: 'Which is NOT mentioned…', 'all of the following EXCEPT'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Circle the NOT/EXCEPT first. Find the list or sentence that three options come from and tick each one you can see in the passage. The option you cannot find, or that the passage contradicts, is the answer.

example.q: Passage lists steps, carvings and shaded platforms as stepwell features. Which is NOT mentioned: steps, carvings, platforms, wooden roofs?
example.solution: Wooden roofs — the only feature not in the passage.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Inference ('It can be inferred / the author implies')
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem uses infer, imply, suggest, 'most probably' or 'what does the author mean by'. The answer is not written word for word.
pyqPatterns.approach: Take the line the question points to and go one small step further. Use the must-be-true test: if the option were false, would the passage stop making sense? Reject word-for-word copies, outside facts, extreme words and invented motives.

example.q: Passage: a farmer's solar pump made water free, he watered longer than needed, and his borewell dropped. What can be inferred?
example.solution: Free power encouraged him to over-pump groundwater. 'Solar pumps always damage groundwater' is too extreme.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Word or phrase meaning in context (synonym / antonym / idiom)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: The stem quotes a word or phrase from the passage and asks its meaning, a synonym or an antonym 'as used in the passage'.

example.q: 'Surely a city that can spend crores on brochures can find the money to lay a single drain.' Tone?

solvedExamples.q:
Read the mini-passage and answer the question that follows.

"Every winter the capital records its worst air of the year, and every winter officials promise action. Filters are distributed, construction is briefly halted, and once the wind changes, the promises are quietly shelved. The cleanup that would matter — cutting crop-stubble burning, electrifying bus fleets, enforcing industrial norms — is announced each year with less conviction than the last."

The central idea of the passage is:
options: Industrial units are the sole source of the capital's smog
Delhi's winter pollution is an annual crisis met with fading commitment
Air filters are the most effective response to winter smog
Changes in wind direction cause Delhi's winter pollution
solvedExamples.solution: The passage contrasts a recurring crisis with a weakening official response: promises made, token steps taken, and the real measures announced 'with less conviction than the last'. **(b)** covers the whole passage at the author's level of criticism. (a) is too extreme — stubble burning and bus fleets are named alongside industry, so industry is not the *sole* source. (c) is contradicted — filters are the *token* step, not the effective one. (d) mentions wind only as the event that ends each episode, not as the cause.

solvedExamples.q:
In the passage below, what does the word **tolerable** mean as used by the author?

"Hospitals report more admissions during hot nights even when the days seem tolerable. Sleep is when the body repairs itself, and a bedroom that never cools denies it that chance."
options: barely bearable
extremely dangerous
shorter than usual
pleasant and comfortable
solvedExamples.solution: The contrast runs: *even when days seem tolerable*, hot nights still send people to hospital. For the contrast to work, tolerable days must be days people can just about cope with — so 'barely bearable' fits, and the sentence keeps working when you plug it in. 'Pleasant and comfortable' is too positive for the contrast ('even when days were pleasant, nights hospitalised people' implies days were pleasant, weakening the author's point about heat). 'Extremely dangerous' contradicts the contrast, and duration is not discussed.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Plug each option into the sentence and keep the *even when* contrast true — only one option survives the plug-in test.
solvedExamples.passage: Hospitals report more admissions during hot nights even when the days seem tolerable. Sleep is when the body repairs itself, and a bedroom that never cools denies it that chance.

solvedExamples.q:
"Small branches in poorer neighbourhoods — precisely those that need them most — are often the first to be marked for closure." (from a passage on public libraries)

Which of the following can be **inferred** from this line?
options: Municipal councils deliberately want to hurt poor neighbourhoods
Rich neighbourhoods have no libraries at all
All small library branches will eventually be closed
The libraries that are most needed face the greatest risk of being shut
solvedExamples.solution: One step from the line: branches in poor areas are small, small branches are closed first, and those areas need libraries most → the most-needed branches face the highest closure risk — **(d)**. (a) adds a motive ('deliberately want to hurt') — the passage blames budgets, not malice. (b) goes outside the line; nothing is said about rich neighbourhoods lacking libraries. (c) turns 'often the first' into 'all… eventually', an extreme the passage never supports.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Verbatim copy = detail, one logical step = inference, added intent/scale = wrong. Rank the options by their distance from the line.

practice.q: Which of the following best states the central idea of the passage?
options: White-painted roofs are the only effective defence against summer heat
Rural areas are warming faster than cities because of deforestation
Cities trap heat through their own construction, but deliberate design changes can reverse it
Global warming will make Indian cities uninhabitable within a few decades
practice.solution: Para 1 explains how city building materials and design create the heat island; para 2 gives its uneven consequences; para 3 argues that local design measures work and ends 'can plan itself out of one'. **(c)** covers this. (a) narrows to one solution although the passage lists several, and 'only' is extreme. (b) reverses the passage — cities are hotter than villages, and deforestation is not discussed. (d) exaggerates beyond the passage and blames global warming, which para 1 explicitly limits.
practice.shortcut: Theme = opening problem + closing claim. The passage frames heat as a *design* outcome and ends on remake-ability — that pair is the idea.
practice.passage:
Cities are quietly getting hotter than the countryside that surrounds them, and the gap is measured every night. On a summer evening, a village a few kilometres outside a metropolis may cool to a comfortable twenty-six degrees while the city itself still holds thirty-three. This difference, known as the urban heat island effect, arises not from global warming alone but from the way cities are built. Concrete, asphalt and brick absorb solar energy all day and release it slowly after sunset, so the city never truly cools. Fewer trees mean less shade and less of the cooling that water escaping from leaves provides. Waste heat from air conditioners, vehicles and industry adds a further burden.

The consequences fall unevenly. The poorest residents often live in dense, poorly ventilated neighbourhoods with tin roofs that turn bedrooms into ovens, and they cannot afford the electricity that cooling demands. Studies in several Indian cities have linked heat waves to falling productivity among construction and delivery workers, whose shifts rarely move to the cooler hours. Night-time heat is particularly dangerous because sleep is when the body repairs itself; hospitals report more admissions during hot nights even when the days seem tolerable.

Solutions need not wait for global action. Painting roofs white, mandating reflective materials for new construction, restoring ponds and planting street trees can lower local temperatures measurably within a single season. Ahmedabad's heat action plan, which pairs early warnings with cool-roof subsidies, has become a model studied by other developing countries. What these measures share is a simple insight: heat islands are created by design choices, and design choices can be remade. The city that planned itself into a heat trap can plan itself out of one.

(a) describes a para-2 problem about *day* shifts of workers, not nights. (c) is never said — the passage says the poor cannot afford electricity. (d) distorts the point about admissions being higher, not restricted, at night.
practice.shortcut: Anchor 'sleep' in para 2 and read the sentence — the answer is inside the 'because' clause.

practice.q: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?
options: Gig Work: Flexibility Gained, Protection Pending
The Coming Collapse of the Platform Economy
Why Employees Prefer Offices Over Factories
How Mobile Apps Deliver Food to Millions
practice.solution: The passage's two halves: flexibility is real (para 1), but risk and legal exclusion fall on workers (paras 1–2), and rules must catch up (para 3). **(a)** compresses exactly this. (b) is contradicted — the author says such work 'will grow'. (c) is never discussed; the factory comparison is about which laws exist, not what employees prefer. (d) narrows to the example in the opening sentence.
practice.shortcut: Title test: cover every paragraph, add nothing, no stance stronger than the author's — only (b) survives all three.
practice.passage:
The app has changed not only how we order food but what it means to have a job. Across the world, millions now earn through platforms that assign work task by task: a ride, a delivery, a design project. Companies celebrate this flexibility, and for some workers it is real — a student can drive between lectures, a parent can log off when the school day ends. Yet the same arrangement shifts nearly every risk of doing business onto the individual. The platform owns the technology, sets the price and directs the customer to the worker; the worker owns the vehicle, the fuel, the insurance and the idle hours between jobs.

Because a gig worker is classified as an independent partner rather than an employee, she generally falls outside labour laws written for factories and offices. No minimum wage applies to hours spent waiting for a request, no paid leave cushions an illness, and contributions to a pension depend entirely on what the worker chooses, or can afford, to set aside. Several countries are now experimenting with a middle category that would grant platform workers some protections without ending flexible scheduling.

Economists warn that the deeper cost may be invisible: a workforce that cannot plan a month ahead also cannot borrow, train or save with confidence. If algorithms increasingly decide who works and for how much, the question is not whether such work will disappear — it will grow — but whether the rules governing it will grow with it. Societies have rewritten labour law before, when work moved from fields to factories; the same imagination can be applied now.

practice.q: According to the passage, which of the following does the platform NOT provide to the gig worker?
options: The technology that connects worker and customer
The price fixed for each task
Insurance for the worker's vehicle
Directions to the customer
practice.solution: Para 1 assigns technology, price-setting and customer direction to the platform, and lists 'the vehicle, the fuel, the insurance and the idle hours' as what the *worker* owns. Insurance therefore comes from the worker, not the platform — making (c) the correct NOT-provided item. (a), (b) and (d) are each explicitly on the platform's side of the list.
practice.shortcut: NOT-questions: mark each option against the sentence's two-sided list; three options on one side leave the fourth.

practice.q: The passage is primarily concerned with:
options: the declining habit of reading printed books in cities
how public libraries have outgrown predictions of their death by serving wider social needs
the rising cost of coffee in public places
the training that librarians receive in digital services
practice.solution: Para 1: the death prediction 'has aged badly'; para 2: libraries now serve homework, job searches, newspapers, coding clubs; para 3: budgets threaten them, yet 'the case for investment has rarely been stronger' — an institution 'succeeding in both worlds'. (b) covers all three. (a) is conceded only in passing ('borrowing... may have dipped') and is actually part of the mistaken prediction. (c) is an illustration in one clause. (d) is a detail of para 2.
practice.shortcut: Count mentions: libraries' widened social role appears in every paragraph; each wrong option lives in a single clause.
practice.passage:
There was a time when critics announced the death of the public library, confident that the internet had made buildings full of books redundant. The prediction has aged badly. Borrowing of printed books may have dipped in some cities, but library buildings are busier than they were a generation ago — because they have quietly become something more than warehouses for novels. In towns where a cup of coffee costs more than many can spare, the library remains the last indoor public space where no purchase is expected and no one asks you to leave.

Walk into any well-run city library this afternoon and you will find schoolchildren finishing homework at long tables, an unemployed man drafting job applications with a librarian's help, an elderly widow reading newspapers she cannot afford to subscribe to, and a coding club teaching teenagers in a side room. Librarians now spend as much time helping residents access government forms and digital services as they do recommending books.

This evolution has not been painless. Budgets trimmed by municipal councils force difficult choices between opening hours and new acquisitions, and smaller branches in poorer neighbourhoods — precisely those that need them most — are often the first to be marked for closure. Yet the case for investment has rarely been stronger. A society that worries about loneliness, digital exclusion and unequal schooling already owns an institution that addresses all three, staffed by professionals trained to help. The library needs not nostalgia but recognition: it is not a relic of the print age barely surviving; it is one of the few public institutions succeeding in both worlds.

help residents with official paperwork and online services as much as with books
have stopped recommending books altogether
are replaced by coding clubs in side rooms

practice.shortcut: Match the balance in the sentence: 'as much X as Y' means both continue — options that delete either half are wrong.

For most of the last century, rice and wheat pushed millets off Indian plates. Government buying, cheap ration-shop grain and the prestige attached to 'white' cereals made coarse grains look like food for the poor. Farmers followed the market, and the area under jowar, bajra and ragi shrank steadily.

Farmers in parts of Himachal Pradesh have begun renting beehives each spring. They place the boxes among their apple trees for a few weeks and return them after the flowers fade. The reason is simple: the wild bees that once did this work free of charge have become scarce.

Scientists point to several causes. Heavy use of pesticides kills bees directly, and orchards planted with a single crop leave few wild flowers to feed them once the fruit blossom is over. Warmer winters also disturb the match between flowering time and the insects' active season.

Renting hives helps, but it is costly, and the hired bees do not reach every orchard. Some villages have tried a cheaper approach: they leave strips of wild flowers along field edges and spray only in the evening, when bees are resting. Early results suggest that such steps bring wild pollinators back within a few seasons. The lesson is that nature's free services are free only as long as we protect them.

practice.q: Which title best suits the passage?

A History of Road Accidents in India
How Metro Rail Changed Indian Cities

Indian cities spend large sums on flyovers, yet the most common journey in any city begins and ends on foot. Despite this, footpaths are often broken, blocked by parked vehicles or taken over by shops, forcing walkers onto the road beside fast traffic.

Long before piped water reached the towns of Gujarat and Rajasthan, people built stepwells. A stepwell is a deep pit lined with stone, with flights of steps leading down to the water. As the level fell during the dry months, people simply walked further down to reach it. practice.q: How often did the cooperative pay its members?
options: Every day

practice.passage:
When the women of Rampur formed a milk cooperative, only twelve households joined. Each morning they brought their milk to a single shed, where it was measured, tested for fat and poured into a shared cooling tank. Before this, a private trader had collected milk from their doorsteps, paid a fixed low price regardless of quality, and often delayed payment for weeks.

The cooperative changed three things. Payment was now linked to the fat content, so families that fed their animals well earned more. Money was paid every ten days, directly into bank accounts opened in the women's own names. And because the milk was cooled at once, less of it turned sour on the way to the dairy.

Within four years the membership had grown to over two hundred households. The members say the biggest change is not the extra income but the confidence: women who once stayed silent at village meetings now keep the cooperative's accounts and argue with officials about prices.

practice.q: It can be inferred from the passage that the online services became popular in the town mainly because:
options: they saved people a full day's trip to the district headquarters
people enjoyed spending time at the cyber café
the online forms were shorter than the paper forms
the café owner was a retired schoolteacher

It left at six in the morning and came back at seven in the evening, so anyone who needed to visit a government office lost a full day's wages for a task that might take twenty minutes.
